name: simd-sort (AVX2 and AVX-512F quicksort, Wojciech Mula)
workload: Sorting arrays of uint32_t (10k to 20M elements) with random, ascending and descending inputs; the speed program times std::sort against a scalar quicksort and the SIMD quicksorts.
claimed_speedup: AVX2 quicksort vs std::sort, random input: 1.91x at 1M elements and 1.96x at 20M on Skylake i7-6700; 1.78x and 1.88x on Haswell i7-4770. AVX-512F quicksort on Xeon Phi 7210 (Knights Landing): 1.39x at 1M and 1.77x at 20M, but only 1.18x at 10k. The repo's scalar quicksort is 1.23-1.33x on the same data. Ratios are the numbers printed in the result files.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.3.0 (from result file names); Makefile: -std=c++11 -mbmi2 -mavx2 (AVX2 build) or -mavx512f (AVX-512 build), speed targets add -O3 -DNDEBUG
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake), Intel Core i7-4770 (Haswell), Intel Xeon Phi 7210 (Knights Landing), per the three files in results/
tradeoffs: x86 only; needs AVX2 or AVX-512F (and BMI2 for some variants); uint32_t keys only; no runtime dispatch; not stable; README calls the code unfinished.
caveats: 2016-2017 results on GCC 5.3.0 and 2016-era CPUs. The standard library behind std::sort is not named (libstdc++ is implied by GCC on Linux but not stated). AVX-512F gains on Knights Landing are modest at small sizes. Superseded in practice by x86-simd-sort and Highway vqsort, which are already catalogued; this repo is the early research code that came out of the author's AVX-512 sorting notes.
found_via: github.com/WojciechMula repository list (author of the 0x80.pl SIMD blog); the 0x80.pl and lemire.me blog hosts could not be resolved from this environment, so the evidence is the repo's own results/ files

name: qAverageColor
baseline: serial (scalar C++) average-colour routine in the same repo
workload: Average colour of an RGBA8 image (synthetic 10-megapixel image in the table; 3840x2160 image in the write-up) using psadbw byte-sum accumulation in SSE4.2, AVX2 and AVX-512 paths.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.2.1; CMakeLists.txt: Release build with -march=native, C++17
tradeoffs: x86 only (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512 paths plus serial fallback); RGBA8 input only; 64-bit accumulators so no overflow below about 69 billion megapixels; a snippet-sized library, not a general image toolkit.
caveats: The baseline is the author's own serial loop (written with _bextr_u64 and built with -march=native), not a library such as OpenCV. Write-up numbers for the i7-7500U (about 2.6x SSE, 4.1x AVX2 on 3840x2160) differ from the table (2.85x and 4.41x on 10 megapixels). Results date from 2019-2021. The speedup depends heavily on the CPU (AVX2 only 2.6x on the i9-7900X).
found_via: github.com/Wunkolo repository list; the README is a blog-style write-up inspired by Wojciech Mula's 'SIMDized sum of all bytes in the array' note (0x80.pl, not reachable from this environment)

name: fastvalidate-utf-8
baseline: scalar C UTF-8 validator (validate_utf8 in benchmarks/benchmark.c, copied in part from Guava, with an ASCII fast path)
workload: Validating 64 KiB buffers: pure ASCII input and random-looking UTF-8; cycles per input byte.
claimed_speedup: Random-looking UTF-8: 0.702 cycles/byte (SSE validate_utf8_fast) and 0.448 (AVX) vs 10.967 for the scalar validator (about 15.6x and 24.5x, derived from page data). ASCII input: 0.704 and 0.450 vs 1.256 cycles/byte (about 1.8x and 2.8x, derived from page data); the ASCII-path variants reach 0.088.
hardware: Intel Skylake processor (exact model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 309 stars; a modified version sped up Scylla (per README)
tradeoffs: Header-only C; x64 with SSE (and AVX variants) only, no ARM; no runtime dispatch; a demonstration library, not meant for production.
caveats: README marks the library obsolete as of 2022 and points to simdutf (already catalogued), which carries the newer lookup algorithm. Benchmark CPU is named only by microarchitecture and the GCC version is missing, so tier C. The ASCII rows favour schemes that skip ASCII quickly (the author says so). Numbers are from the README; the two blog posts it cites (lemire.me, 2018) could not be opened.
found_via: github.com/lemire repository list filtered by 'simd'; README cites Lemire's blog posts 'Validating UTF-8 strings using as little as 0.7 cycles per byte' (2018-05-16) and the AVX edition (2018-10-19)

name: validateutf8-experiments (lookup UTF-8 validation, Keiser and Lemire)
baseline: scalar UTF-8 validators in the repo benchmark: the DFA variants (dfa, dfa2, dfa3, dfa4), the 'fushia' rows and utf8lib (dependencies/utf8_v2_3_4)
workload: Validating examples/hongkong.html (1807 KB) and examples/twitter.json (631 KB) with SSE, AVX2 and NEON validators; GB/s, instructions per byte and branch misses reported.
claimed_speedup: README example, hongkong.html: lookup4 20.934 GB/s vs dfa 0.581, fushia 2.612 and utf8lib 2.570 GB/s (about 36x, 8.0x and 8.1x, derived from page data). twitter.json: lookup4 37.0 GB/s vs dfa 0.582, fushia 2.811 and utf8lib 2.577 (about 64x, 13x and 14x, derived). results/skylake.txt, hongkong.html: lookup4avx 17.081 GB/s vs dfa 0.615, fushia 1.578, utf8lib 0.512. Zwegner's AVX validator is slightly faster than lookup4 on twitter.json (41.029 vs 37.0 GB/s in the README run).
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release, -march=native (/arch:AVX2 on MSVC); Dockerfile uses Ubuntu 20.10 with g++-9 and clang++-9
hardware: README run at about 3.5 GHz and results/skylake.txt at about 3.69 GHz (Skylake, model not stated); results/rome.txt is also checked in. CPU models are not named.
stars_or_usage: 42 stars; algorithm shipped in simdutf (Node.js, Bun, WebKit per the README)
tradeoffs: Research code for validation only (no transcoding); x64 SSE/AVX2 and ARM64 NEON paths; README says not for production use.
caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed paper cited in the README (Keiser and Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 2021), which could not be opened here; the repo itself has no CPU model or compiler version in its text. No LICENSE file was visible in the repo listing, so it is marked reference. The production form of this algorithm is simdutf, which is already catalogued.

name: utf8lut
baseline: scalar slow path of the same library (-b=0), a scalar UTF-8 to UTF-16 and UTF-16 to UTF-8 converter
workload: Converting about 1 MB buffers from RAM to RAM, UTF-8 to UTF-16 (decode) and UTF-16 to UTF-8 (encode), on a random code-point dataset (33% each of 1, 2 and 3 byte) and the Russian novel 'War and Peace' in fb2 format; CPU cycles per byte.
claimed_speedup: Fast path (-b=3 -m=2) vs scalar slow path, cycles per byte (core conversion by rdtsc): random decode 1.65 vs 15.3 (about 9.3x), random encode 0.74 vs 9.9 (about 13x), fb2 decode 1.00 vs 9.10 (about 9.1x), fb2 encode 0.68 vs 4.89 (about 7.2x); ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: not stated for the table; build instructions say -mssse3 -std=c++11 for non-MSVC, scripts for MSVC, MinGW and GCC
tradeoffs: x86 with SSSE3 only; a large lookup table that barely fits the CPU cache, so speed depends on the code-point length distribution (uniform random is the worst case); the fast path needs more than 99% of characters handled to pay off; non-BMP characters use the slow path; the iconv-style interface deviates from the spec.
caveats: The comparison is against the library's own scalar path, not against iconv, ICU or another incumbent; the README points to a blog article with broader comparisons that could not be opened (dirtyhandscoding.github.io host not resolvable). Compiler and flags for the table are not given. README calls it mainly a proof of concept. Repo migrated from Bitbucket and last changed in 2020.
found_via: link in the README of WojciechMula/utf16utf8 ('utf8lut: Vectorized UTF-8 converter') which points to the dirtyhandscoding.github.io blog

name: corvus (SIMD statistical special functions)
baseline: vendor scalar libm called per element: UCRT (Windows), Apple libm x86 and Apple libm arm64 (std::cos, std::sin, std::erf, std::lgamma)
workload: Batched span-in span-out evaluation of 10^6 doubles for cos, sin, exp, log, log1p, erf, erfc and lgamma, timed against calling the system libm function for each element; median of repeated timings after warm-up.
claimed_speedup: cos and sin: 5.50x and 5.58x (Zen 4 vs UCRT, 1.6 ns/element), 4.87x and 4.98x (Kaby Lake vs Apple x86 libm), 3.27x and 3.21x (M1 vs Apple arm64 libm, single gated run); README: 3.2-5.6x ahead of every vendor libm measured. lgamma: 1.5-5.2x vs UCRT but 0.2-0.9x vs Apple libm. exp 1.20x/0.65x/1.28x. log runs at 0.2-0.64x of the libm (slower by design, it is correctly rounded).
compiler_and_flags: clang-cl Release (Windows); Apple Clang 15 Release preset with Ninja (macOS); Google Highway as the SIMD backend with runtime dispatch (AVX3_ZEN4, AVX2, NEON asserted per target)
hardware: Ryzen 7 (Zen 4, exact SKU not given) on Windows 11; Intel i7-7820HQ (Kaby Lake) on macOS 13.7; Apple M1 Mac Mini. 5% ambient-CPU gate on Zen 4 and Kaby Lake, 10% gate on M1.
tradeoffs: C++20 with a std::span API; Highway (Apache-2.0) is a build dependency; accuracy-first double-double kernels, so the README says accuracy is the claim and throughput is not; the margin varies a lot by function and by which libm is the baseline.
caveats: Single-author first-party measurements. The M1 column is marked REPORTED, NOT PUBLISHED (single gated run) and two function families are listed as not reproducible yet (section 5 of PERFORMANCE.md). Ratios across libms are not comparable by the author's own rule. Only cos and sin clearly win everywhere; log and log1p lose, exp is mixed. Windows numbers use clang-cl only; no GCC or MSVC build was measured.
found_via: github.com/topics/avx2 (C++, sorted by recently updated) listing; README and PERFORMANCE.md read directly; not a blog-sourced find
